title: Improved State Readout in NV Centers using Regression Models and Rabi Driving
abstract: Readout of state populations in nitrogen-vacancy centers from fluorescence measurements at room-temperature is routinely achieved via contrast-based calibration. The fidelities achieved by this conventional approach are limited by reducing the dynamical fluorescence behaviour of the NV center to a scalar value, and calculating the population of each possible state independently. To address these limitations, we use regression models trained on experimental data to map the fluorescence signals onto ideal simulated populations. Additionally, we enhance the informational content of the fluorescence signals by performing measurements during induced Rabi oscillations. Our results demonstrate that including these dynamical signals significantly reduces state readout errors across multiple tested models. Notably, linear ridge regression performs nearly on par with a non-linear kernel-based model, showing that simple models already capture the relevant mapping between the enhanced fluorescence signals and the underlying state populations. This data-driven approach provides a robust alternative that achieves higher fidelities than conventional calibration in our setting, paving the way for high-fidelity state readout in solid-state quantum registers.
summary: This paper presents an improved method for reading out the state populations of NV center qubits at room temperature by employing data-driven regression models trained on experimental fluorescence signals. By incorporating measurements during induced Rabi oscillations, the authors show that these machine learning approaches achieve significantly higher readout fidelities compared to standard contrast calibration techniques. This paves the way for more reliable solid-state quantum memory and processing.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving high-fidelity state readout of quantum populations in Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers at room temperature.
main_result: Data-driven regression models, especially those incorporating dynamical Rabi oscillation measurements, significantly outperform conventional contrast calibration methods for state readout fidelity.
method: The authors employ machine learning techniques, specifically Ridge and Kernel Ridge Regression, to map raw fluorescence signals onto ideal simulated quantum populations.
model_or_system: The system utilizes NV centers in diamond as a solid-state two-qubit quantum register. Readout relies on measuring spin-dependent photoluminescence at room temperature, which is complicated by phonon broadening.
key_observables: Prediction fidelity $F(p^*, \hat{p})$, Mean Squared Error (MSE), and Total Variation Distance (TV distance) comparing predicted populations ($\hat{p}$) to ideal theoretical populations ($p^*$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation; external magnetic field ($B \approx 500	ext{ G}$); inclusion of Rabi oscillation measurements.
main_assumptions: Conventional methods assume simple linear relationships, while the ML approach assumes that a mapping function (approximated by regression) can accurately relate measured signals to true populations.
figures_summary: Figures compare prediction fidelities across various readout models (Contrast vs. Regression) using single-point versus dynamical Rabi measurements; fidelity is shown to improve with more input features and training data size.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares multiple state reconstruction methods—including contrast, matrix inversion, Ridge, and KRR—evaluating their performance by incorporating enhanced measurement protocols derived from Rabi oscillations. The results demonstrate the superior robustness of the data-driven regression approaches.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical bottleneck in solid-state quantum computing: high-fidelity readout. For theorists working on open quantum systems, it provides empirical validation for using advanced ML techniques to model complex measurement backactions and decoherence effects.
